transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2027-06-21 16:00 PDT
Duration: 46 minutes
Attendees: Sofia Patel (Redwood AE), Mateo Ruiz (Redwood SE), Hannah Lee (Redwood SE), Elena Brooks (CTO Montage), Rajesh Singh (Head of Platform), Maya Thompson (PM), Darius Cole (SRE)

Summary (auto): quick intake to map availability requirements, incident tolerance expectations, and legal/contract constraints around SLAs and auditability. Plan: pilot + benchmarks + SLA draft.

00:00 - Sofia: hey everyone, thanks for taking the time. we wanted to do a quick intake to understand what resilience and incident tolerance looks like for montage. i'll hand it over to elena to frame the business requirements.
00:18 - Elena: yeah thanks, so our two big concerns are user facing latency under 200–300ms for primary flows and secondarily if a region goes down we need routing to shift within under 90s. also we have strict PHI requirements, we need audit logs and customer-managed keys.
00:36 - Rajesh: to add, our contract teams want an availability target of 99.95% for inference endpoints with clear RTO expectations. we also need a fallback plan in case the top-level model is slow or degrades in quality.
00:50 - Mateo: got it. two quick clarifications: when you say routing to shift within 90 seconds, do you mean full traffic cutover or a staged rollout? and on the 99.95% - is that rollup across regions or per-region?
01:12 - Darius: we want automatic cutover, basically drain in-region and failover. but we'll accept staged if it shortens risk. for SLA we want it across the product endpoint, not per-region, contractual.
01:28 - Sofia: okay that helps. for context, Redwood supports a few patterns: hosted with cross-region routing, dedicated pools pinned to customers, and private (VPC/onprem) with a private control plane. each has different tradeoffs for failover speed and auditability.
01:45 - Elena: can you briefly map expected latency and cost tradeoffs? the finance team will push back if costs balloon.
01:55 - Hannah: sure — for hosted cross-region we can push traffic to an adjacent region within tens of seconds with our steering system; p95s depend on model size, but we typically see ~150–300ms for medium sequence gen models. dedicated pools are faster at steady state because of reserved capacity and warm KV caches but cost more. private onprem gives you max control but we have to coordinate network egress and you'll be responsible for runbook ops.
02:25 - Maya: when you say warm KV caches — what happens to session tokens and state during failover? any risk of context loss?
02:38 - Mateo: good question. we maintain per-request KV cache in the serving layer. for cross-region failover there is inevitably some cold-start for KV in the second region; we mitigate with prefix caching and pre-warm hooks during canary/rollout. there's always a small window where responses may lose a few tokens of context, we try to bound that.
03:02 - Rajesh: acceptable if you can quantify it in runbook terms and include in the SLA appendix.
03:12 - Sofia: noted. on the contractual SLA side redd — sorry redwood typically offers 99.9% for hosted standard, 99.95% for dedicated with reserved capacity, and private deployments are negotiable with SLAs baked into the enterprise agreement. we can — we should prototype language and show penalty structures.
03:40 - Elena: 99.9 vs 99.95 is a big delta for us. what are the failure modes that drive the difference?
03:50 - Hannah: most delta comes from capacity constraints and cross-region network latencies. dedicated reserve gives you guaranteed GPUs and pre-warmed caches. hosted shares pools, so during noisy neighbor events or sudden traffic spikes you may see degradation unless you have a reservation or burst contract.
04:12 - Darius: do you have on-call escalation and audit trails for incidents? we need full audit logs for the last seven years per compliance.
04:22 - Sofia: we provide audit logs with Dedicated and Private. Hosted includes limited request logs and tracing, but for full SAML/SSO audit and long retention, dedicated or private is recommended. we'll share the security package.
04:40 - Elena: can you support KMS/HSM for key management? our legal requires customer-managed keys for token encryption.
04:48 - Mateo: yes, we integrate with customer KMS for both dedicated and private options; hosted can also use bring-your-own-key but in hosted it's a managed integration with audit hooks. our docs will show supported providers (AWS KMS, GCP KMS, and HSM via vault).
05:10 - Maya: another question on fallback model tiers: we need graceful degradation from our high-quality gen model to a cheaper, smaller checkpoint when latency spikes. can you do automatic model fallback without changing API semantics?
05:22 - Hannah: yes, we have policy-based fallback. you can configure per-route policies: e.g. if p95 > 350ms or error-rate > 1% then route to a quantized smaller model. the SDK surface is the same, but you'll see differences in output characteristics and we recommend adding an eval/quality guardrail to detect regressions.
05:47 - Elena: so the platform will do live rollback if quality drops? who owns the safety net?
05:53 - Mateo: Redwood can do automatic fallback and optionally automatic rollback. typical enterprise setup: Redwood triggers fallback, not rollback, and then notifies your oncall; you can configure automatic rollback only after manual sign-off. it reduces risk of removing useful features.
06:12 - Rajesh: in terms of detection, what signals do you evaluate? latency only or also quality/semantic checks?
06:20 - Hannah: we look at latency, error rates, and can run lightweight quality checks against a small golden prompt set in the control plane. you can push custom prompt sets so the guards reflect your domain.
06:34 - Darius: what's the expected time to detect and execute fallback? and are rollbacks auditable?
06:40 - Mateo: detection is near real-time for latency and error rates (seconds to a minute). executing policy — like model-switch — usually completes in 30–90s depending on cache priming. all actions are auditable in the console with logs and traces.
07:02 - Speaker 1: (mumble) are there limits on how many regions you can failover to?
07:08 - Hannah: no hard limit, but practical constraints exist: model artifacts need to be available in the region, and cross-region replication might take time if it's not already replicated. for private deployments you manage artifact replication.
07:24 - Elena: on the legal side, are there SLA credits or penalties? our procurement folks want clear liquidated damages.
07:32 - Sofia: yes, we'll include a proposed credit schedule. typical example: below 99.95% we offer 5% service credit, incremental for lower tiers; exact terms are negotiable for enterprise contracts. we'll send a draft SLA.
07:50 - Rajesh: can you support blackhole routing or just steer? in some failure modes we prefer rejecting traffic from degraded regions to avoid stale data.
08:00 - Mateo: you can configure the routing policy — fail-open (redirect) or fail-closed (reject). we also support weighted traffic split during partial degradation.
08:12 - Maya: what's the recommended chaos testing cadence? we need to pass internal audits.
08:18 - Hannah: we recommend quarterly chaos tests for region failovers and monthly smoke tests for model fallbacks. Redwood can help run an initial chaos run and collect metrics for your audit team.
08:32 - Darius: we will need runbook examples: exact commands for failover, expected monitoring thresholds, escalation path, and contact list. do you have templates?
08:41 - Sofia: yes — we have runbook templates and incident playbooks for Dedicated and Private. we'll provide a starter pack.
08:50 - Elena: i want to understand the pilot shape — what does the 72-hour canary look like?
08:58 - Mateo: we propose a staged pilot: 1) baseline run on hosted for 24h with synthetic and real traffic, 2) migrate a slice of production to a dedicated pool for 24h to validate warm caches and latency, 3) run failover drills + simulated region outage for 24h and capture metrics. total ~72h.
09:22 - Rajesh: what metrics will we capture?
09:26 - Hannah: p50/p95/p99 latency, throughput (qps), error rates, token cost, model quality delta on a golden set, failover duration, and KV cold-start penalty.
09:36 - Maya: we will need to share sample dataset and NDA? any PII concerns?
09:41 - Sofia: yes, we'll sign the updated NDA; for pilot please send redacted datasets or use our secure upload in the private pilot environment.
09:52 - Elena: regarding data retention, can you make logs immutable for X days?
09:57 - Mateo: for Dedicated and Private we can configure retention and immutability policy; hosted is limited but we provide paid long-term retention add-ons.
10:06 - Darius: in a worst-case catastrophic region failure, do you support cold standby in another cloud provider?
10:12 - Hannah: multi-cloud cold standby is possible but requires artifact replication and network peering; it's typically part of an enterprise private deployment. for hosted we usually recommend adjacent-region hot standby in same cloud provider for latency reasons.
10:28 - Rajesh: cost modeling — can you model the cost delta of a 99.95% SLA vs 99.9%? finance wants numbers.
10:36 - Sofia: yes, Redwood Optimize will produce cost/perf tradeoffs and recommendations. Mateo will work with you on a cost model after we get your traffic profile.
10:46 - Rajesh: ok send the model please.
10:48 - Sofia: noted.
11:00 - Elena: i want to raise one more compliance point: we will need an attestation that all access to logs is RBAC-controlled and that we can get a per-user audit trail.
11:10 - Hannah: our console supports RBAC with SSO groups and per-action audit logs for Dedicated and Private. we'll include an example mapping in the security docs.
11:22 - Maya: what about data residency — can you keep inference processing within eu-west-1 for eu users?
11:27 - Mateo: yes, with region pinning you can force requests to eu-west-1 and disable cross-region fallback for those endpoints if residency constraints demand it. it's a policy toggle.
11:40 - Darius: how do you version model artifacts across regions so we don't get mismatched behavior during failover?
11:47 - Mateo: we use an immutable artifact versioning and manifest. the control plane ensures that only compatible model variants are chosen for failover. mismatches are prevented by semantic checks and a compatibility matrix.
12:05 - Elena: quick nit: we've seen call transcripts where product names get munged; is there a glossary you can share?
12:11 - Sofia: yes, we'll include a short glossary plus the security package and runbooks.
12:19 - Maya: any references you can share — case studies for healthcare customers?
12:23 - Hannah: we have a case with Lumina Health where we ran region failovers during a maintenance window; we'll send a one-pager.
12:33 - Rajesh: if we move forward with a pilot, what are the gating criteria?
12:37 - Sofia: typically: SLA acceptance, security review passed, sample data uploaded, and a signed pilot SOW. we'll draft a minimal SOW for you.
12:46 - Elena: timeline-wise procurement moved fast; can we target pilot kickoff in the first week of july?
12:51 - Sofia: yes, target week of 2027-07-05 works.
12:56 - Maya: one more question on metrics exposed: can we stream traces to our datadog?
13:03 - Mateo: yes, we support exporting traces and metrics to Datadog, Splunk, or exporting via S3 for long-term storage.
13:12 - Darius: for canary runs will you provide runbooks we can execute to trigger failover?
13:18 - Hannah: yes, and we'll run the first drill jointly so we can tweak thresholds.
13:24 - Sofia: i'll recap next steps now.
13:26 - Sofia: recap: we'll share the SOC2/security package and glossary (Sofia), Mateo will schedule the 72-hour benchmark and draft the pilot plan, we'll send a draft SLA with credit schedule, montage will provide traffic profile and sample dataset. pilot kickoff planned w/c 2027-07-05.
13:48 - Elena: that's good — thanks.
13:50 - Rajesh: we'll await the docs and schedule.
13:54 - Sofia: thanks everyone, we'll follow up in email with links to the security pack and SOW.
14:00 - (call ends)
